title: Context siphon bench log - Maya
content:
Quick summary:
- Short experiment log exploring a weird throughput/latency pattern I nicknamed 'context siphon' — when a small set of requests with long contexts appear, they seem to pull KV cache residency and cause following short-context requests to degrade (p95 jumps) for ~20-40s.
- Setup: single A100-80GB box, model redwood-open-7b-4k (fp16), continuous batching enabled, default batch_timeout 4ms, prefix caching on, per-tenant KV cache (config: max_entries=5000, ttl=300s).
- Goal: reproduce reliably and capture telemetry (KV hit-rate timeline, per-request seq_len, batch composition).

Notes and environment:
- Machine: a100-80gb (ubuntu 22.04, driver 535), gVisor not used, nvidia-smi logs collected.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.42.3 (local build from PR 1024), batcher = dynamic (max_batch_tokens=65536).
- Load generator: custom harness (go) that can emit mix of long/short contexts with controlled inter-arrival.
- Model config: context window 4096, typical prompt lengths used: short=32 tokens, long=1800 tokens.
- Concurrency: 18 workers hitting endpoint concurrently unless noted.

Test matrix (selected runs):
1) Baseline steady short-context flow (QPS 120, all reqs = 32 tokens).
2) Single long-context injection (one request of 1800 tokens at t=60s) into steady short flow.
3) Repeated long bursts: 5 long requests spaced by 2s each.
4) High-mix: 20% long, 80% short at QPS 140.

Raw observations (from traces):
- Baseline: steady p50 ~ 48ms, p95 ~ 120ms, p99 ~ 240ms. KV cache hit-rate ~ 87% steady.
- Single long injection: immediate spike — the long req itself p95 ~ 2.6s (expected), but more interesting: following 12-30s window, short requests p95 increases to 380-520ms (x3-4), p50 unaffected. KV hit-rate drops to ~52% during that window, gradually recovering to baseline over ~35s.
- Repeated long bursts: recovery time longer (~60s), p95 oscillates in 300-900ms range for short requests.
- High-mix run: steady-state p95 sits at ~280ms (worse than baseline but stable), KV hit-rate at ~64%.

Instrumentation notes (what I logged):
- Per-request: seq_len, batch_id, batch_token_count, batch_members, start_ts, end_ts, kv_cache_hits, kv_cache_misses, evictions_triggered.
- Host: free GPU memory, nvtop snapshots, kernel logs for OOM/evictions.
- Traces show that after the long request completes, the runtime triggers a mini-eviction sweep (evicting ~8-15% of entries) to make room for the long KV entries; these evictions are correlated with short-request cache misses.

Hypothesis: 
1) Long contexts allocate large KV cache segments (per request/session) that force the eviction policy to free contiguous entries, which are not exactly the least-recently-used for the short-request working set. The eviction pattern effectively 'siphons' working-set entries from the short-reqs.
2) Recovery time is dominated by the rate at which short-request traffic re-populates the cache and by the eviction cooldown (we have a guard to avoid immediate re-allocation).

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Logged evictions during (and immediately after) long requests: evicted_entries_count spikes from baseline ~12 to ~160.
- Evicted entries map to tenant-specific prefixes that the short requests frequently used (checked via hashed prefix ids).
- When I disabled the eviction cooldown (dev flag), recovery was faster, but this caused oscillation under heavier mixed load (more thrashing).

Quick experiments I ran to validate mitigation ideas:
A) Increase per-tenant max_entries from 5k to 10k — result: reduced p95 bump on single-long injection (p95 peaked ~220ms instead of 380ms), but under high-mix this simply shifted problem (overall memory footprint grew; risk of OOM with more tenants).
B) Preferential eviction policy: mark short-req working-set items as protected for N seconds — result: promising for single injections (peak lower) but introduced starvation when many long contexts exist simultaneously.
C) Batch-timeout tuning: increasing batch_timeout to 8ms reduced the frequency of combining long+short in same batch, lowering the observed cross-effect (p95 reduced by ~15%), but increases base latency and worsens cost.

A small ascii timeline from a representative single-long injection run (timestamps relative to start):
0s: short flow steady (p95 120ms)
60s: long request enters (occupies KV chunk, runtime starts writing large KV)
61-63s: long request completes (p95 2.6s). Evictions_event burst logged at 62s.
62-95s: short requests p95 elevated (380-520ms), KV hit_rate dips to 52%
95-130s: gradual recovery, hit rate back to 80%+

Questions / open investigation items:
- Are evictions contiguous ranges because of internal allocation strategy? Need heap/allocator dumps to verify physical layout. (Assign to @Ibrahim to grab live arena dumps when we re-run).
- Does tenant isolation (per-tenant LRU) completely avoid siphoning across tenants? I suspect this is per-tenant already but TTL/size interplay is the culprit. Need to run cross-tenant mix.
- Could we adopt a two-tier cache (small fast LRU for hot prefixes + large background store) — tradeoffs?
- How will Dedicated customers with reserved pool behave differently (b/c they might have pinned capacity)? Include dedicated-run.

Next runs to schedule (short backlog):
- Re-run single-long injection with per-tenant isolation flag toggled (config toggle in PR 1024). Capture full heap diffs. (WIP: ticket LIN-2117)
- Cross-tenant run: tenantA long burst, tenantB short flow — measure cross-impact (isolation effectiveness).
- Eviction policy A/B: try 'soft-protect' for items touched in last 5s vs 20s and measure thrash points.
- Simulate N=50 tenants with random long/short mixes (scale test) to see worst-case memory footprint.

Operational notes / suggestions for short-term guardrails:
- Add alerting for sustained KV eviction spikes > 100/sec per host for > 10s (we saw 160 per single long request).
- Provide a config knob on Dedicated for higher per-tenant cache limits to avoid noisy neighbor within a committed pool.
- Documentation: note that long-context requests have outsized impact on cache residency; warn customers who use long contexts at scale.

Notes-to-self (todo):
- Clean up instrumentation traces and push to s3://perf-archive/context-siphon/ (Ibrahim will help with upload).
- Draft a short Slack post in #perf-debug summarizing the siphon phenomenon + recommended short-term guardrails.
- Pair with Rowan to add a compact telemetry metric: "kv_eviction_spike" that tags tenant and batch_id.

Final quick takeaways (for product folks):
- Long contexts can degrade short-request p95 for tens of seconds due to eviction behavior (not just raw GPU time).
- Tuning per-tenant cache sizes or changing eviction policies mitigates but doesn't eliminate the problem under high-mix loads.
- Larger architectural options (two-tier cache, isolation guarantees) might be needed for heavy mixed workloads (especially for multi-tenant hosted mode).

If anyone wants to reproduce: leave a note and I'll hand over the harness + run script. Results and raw traces in linked artifacts (PR has flags to enable verbose evictions).

-- Maya

(rough/working notes, not polished; will move to a proper perf doc if this tracks as a real customer-risk finding)
